questions.stem: What does an arrow in a food chain show?
options: Which way the animals travel
The direction energy moves as one organism is eaten by another
Which animal is stronger
The order the animals were discovered
questions.explanation: Arrows point from the food to the feeder — the direction the energy flows. Drawing them the wrong way is the single most common error in this topic.

questions.stem: What is a producer?
options: An organism that breaks down dead material
An animal that eats plants
An organism that makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis
An animal that eats other animals
questions.explanation: Producers such as plants and algae build their own food from light. Everything else in the chain ultimately depends on them.

questions.stem: What is a herbivore?
options: An animal that eats only meat
An animal that eats both plants and meat
An organism that decomposes dead matter
An animal that eats only plants
questions.explanation: Herbivores eat plants. Meat-only eaters are carnivores and mixed feeders are omnivores.

questions.stem: What is a decomposer?
options: An animal that eats only living plants
An organism that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil
An animal at the top of a food chain
A plant that makes its own food
questions.explanation: Decomposers such as fungi and many bacteria recycle nutrients from dead organisms back into the ecosystem.

questions.stem: Where does the energy in almost every food chain originally come from?
options: Water
The Sun
The soil
Decomposers
questions.explanation: Producers capture light energy from the Sun. Soil supplies minerals and water, not energy.
questions.teaching:
Trace any food chain backwards far enough and you reach the point where energy first entered living systems.

Plants and algae capture light and store it as chemical energy in glucose. A herbivore eating them gets some of it; a predator eating the herbivore gets some of that. At every transfer most is lost as heat, which is why chains are rarely more than four or five steps long. Almost every ecosystem on Earth traces back this way, with one striking exception: deep-sea vent communities, which run on chemical energy from the Earth instead.

questions.stem: What is a food web?
options: A map showing where animals live
Many food chains linked together in an ecosystem
A single line of organisms that eat each other
A list of all plants in an area
questions.explanation: A web shows the interconnected feeding relationships, which is far more realistic than a single chain — most animals eat more than one thing.

questions.stem: What is a consumer?
options: An organism that only breaks down waste
An organism that lives in the soil
An organism that gets energy by eating other organisms
An organism that makes its own food
questions.explanation: Consumers cannot make their own food, so they eat others. Producers make their own.

questions.stem: In the chain grass → grasshopper → frog → snake, what is the grasshopper?
options: A producer
A secondary consumer
A decomposer
A primary consumer
questions.explanation: The first consumer in a chain is the primary consumer. The frog, eating the grasshopper, is secondary.

questions.stem: What is a predator?
options: An animal that eats only plants
An animal that hunts and eats other animals
An animal that is hunted
An organism that makes its own food
questions.explanation: Predators hunt; the animals they hunt are prey. An animal can be both, depending on who it is compared with.

questions.stem: What is an ecosystem?
options: A single food chain
All the living things in an area together with their non-living surroundings
Only the animals living in an area
Only the plants living in an area
questions.explanation: An ecosystem includes organisms plus the physical environment — soil, water, light and temperature.

questions.stem: What is an omnivore?
options: An animal that eats only plants
An animal that eats only meat
An organism that photosynthesises
An animal that eats both plants and animals
questions.explanation: Omnivores have a mixed diet. Humans, pigs and many birds are omnivores.

questions.stem: Which organisms are usually at the base of a food web?
options: Top predators
Decomposers
Herbivores
Producers
questions.explanation: Producers form the base because they bring energy into the ecosystem. Top predators are at the other end.
questions.teaching:
Food webs are usually drawn with energy entering at the bottom and moving upwards, so the base is where energy enters the living world.

That entry point has to be organisms capable of capturing energy from a non-living source — almost always sunlight — and building it into chemical form. Consumers cannot do this; they only pass along energy captured by something else. This is also why there are far more of these organisms by mass than anything above them: only about 10% of energy transfers at each step, so each level up supports much less life than the one below.

questions.stem: What is a habitat?
options: The group an organism belongs to
The time of year an organism breeds
The place where an organism lives
The food an organism eats
questions.explanation: A habitat is where an organism lives — its address. What it does there is its niche.

questions.stem: Roughly how much of the energy at one level passes on to the next?
options: About 90 per cent
All of it
None of it
About 10 per cent
questions.explanation: Most energy is lost as heat, in movement and in undigested waste. Only about a tenth is available to the next level, which is why chains are short.

questions.stem: Which of these is a producer?
options: A seagull
A fungus
Seagrass
A crab
questions.explanation: Seagrass photosynthesises. Fungi are decomposers, and crabs and seagulls are consumers.
questions.teaching:
Every organism in a food web is classified by how it obtains energy, and there are only a few categories.

Organisms that make their own food using light energy sit at the base — plants on land, algae and seagrasses in water. Everything else has to consume something: herbivores eat those food-makers, carnivores eat other consumers, and omnivores do both. Decomposers break down dead material. So the test for this question is simply which option makes its own food rather than eating something else, and that means looking for a photosynthesiser.

questions.stem: In the chain algae → small fish → larger fish → seal, which is the secondary consumer?
options: The small fish
The seal
The algae
The larger fish
questions.explanation: Counting consumers from the producer: small fish is primary, larger fish secondary, seal tertiary.

questions.stem: Why are food chains rarely more than four or five links long?
options: There are not enough species in most ecosystems
Predators refuse to eat other predators
So much energy is lost at each level that little is left to support another
Animals higher up are too large to catch prey
questions.explanation: Only around 10% carries over between levels, so after a few steps there is not enough energy to support another population.

questions.stem: A disease wipes out the rabbits in an area. What is the most likely short-term effect?
options: Every species in the web declines equally
Plants decline because rabbits fertilised them
Only the rabbits' predators are affected, not the plants
Predators that ate rabbits decline, and plants rabbits ate increase
questions.explanation: Removing a species pushes effects both ways: fewer resources for its predators and less pressure on its food.

questions.stem: Why is a food web a better model of an ecosystem than a single food chain?
options: Food webs show the exact number of each animal
Most organisms eat and are eaten by several species
Food webs show how far animals travel
Food chains cannot show producers
questions.explanation: A chain shows one path only. A web captures alternative food sources, which is what makes an ecosystem resilient.

questions.stem: What is likely to happen to a food web if a top predator is removed?
options: The producers immediately die out
Nothing, since top predators eat very little
All consumers become producers
Its prey may increase, putting pressure on the species below them
questions.explanation: Removing predation can let prey populations rise sharply, and the effect cascades down. This is one reason top predators matter out of proportion to their numbers.

questions.stem: Land is cleared for farming and a forest is fragmented. What is the most likely ecological effect?
options: All species benefit from the extra edge habitat
Producers disappear from the region entirely
Food chains become longer
Species that need large connected areas decline
questions.explanation: Fragmentation isolates populations and reduces the range available to wide-ranging species. Some edge species do benefit, but not all.

questions.stem: Why do decomposers matter to producers?
options: They eat the animals that would eat plants
They carry pollen between plants
They release nutrients from dead material back into the soil for plants to use
They provide light energy to plants
questions.explanation: Without decomposition, nutrients would stay locked in dead matter and plant growth would stall.

questions.stem: A pesticide builds up in the bodies of organisms along a food chain. Which group is at greatest risk?
options: Producers
Primary consumers
Decomposers
Top predators
questions.explanation: Bioaccumulation concentrates the chemical at each level, so the highest doses end up in animals at the top.

questions.stem: Introduced foxes and cats have devastated Australian native mammals. Why were the impacts so severe?
options: The predators were much larger than native animals
Native mammals stopped reproducing entirely
The introduced species ate only plants
Native species had not evolved defences against these predators
questions.explanation: Long isolation meant native species lacked appropriate anti-predator behaviour. Both foxes and cats are efficient hunters of small mammals.

questions.stem: Which change would most directly reduce the number of herbivores in a grassland?
options: A prolonged drought that kills much of the grass
An increase in the number of decomposers
A decrease in the number of predators
More rainfall over several seasons
questions.explanation: Herbivores depend directly on plant growth, so losing the producers limits them fastest. Fewer predators would tend to increase herbivore numbers.

questions.stem: In a pyramid of numbers for oak tree → caterpillars → birds, why is the bottom bar narrow?
options: Birds are producers
One large producer can support many small consumers
There is very little energy at the producer level
Oak trees are consumers
questions.explanation: Pyramids of numbers count individuals, so a single huge tree makes a narrow base. A pyramid of biomass would show the usual wide base.

questions.stem: Why is clearing native vegetation along a river especially damaging?
options: It only affects animals that live in trees
It removes habitat, increases erosion and changes conditions in the water
It increases shade over the water, cooling it too much
It increases the number of producers in the river
questions.explanation: Riparian vegetation shades the water, holds banks together and supports both land and water species, so its loss has effects on both sides.

questions.stem: Which statement about competition in an ecosystem is correct?
options: Competition only happens between predators
Competition only occurs between different species
Competition matters only when resources are abundant
Organisms compete for limited resources such as food, water, light and space
questions.explanation: Competition happens within and between species, and it is a major factor limiting how large populations grow.

questions.stem: Sea otters eat sea urchins, which eat kelp. What happens to kelp forests if otters are removed?
options: Urchins decline without otters to disturb them
Nothing, because otters do not eat kelp
Urchin numbers rise and kelp is grazed down
Kelp increases because otters no longer shade it
questions.explanation: This is a classic trophic cascade: the predator's effect reaches two levels down. Otters protect kelp indirectly, by eating what eats it.

questions.stem: Why is biomass usually a better basis for an ecological pyramid than number of individuals?
options: It shows exactly how much energy is transferred
It works only for aquatic ecosystems
It accounts for organisms of very different sizes at the same level
It is easier to measure than counting
questions.explanation: Counting treats an oak and a blade of grass as one each. Biomass reflects the actual material and so lines up better with energy flow, though it is harder to measure.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best show that a river's food web has been damaged by pollution?
options: The river flows more slowly than last year
A sustained fall in the diversity and number of species compared with an unpolluted stretch
The water looks slightly different in colour
One dead fish is found on the bank
questions.explanation: A comparison against a control site over time is what distinguishes a real effect from natural variation. A single observation cannot.

questions.stem: Why can an ecosystem with more species usually cope better with the loss of one of them?
options: More species means more total energy enters the ecosystem
Larger ecosystems never lose species
More species means shorter food chains
Other species can fill similar roles, so energy still flows through the web
questions.explanation: Redundancy in a complex web means alternative feeding pathways exist. A simple chain has no alternative route.

questions.stem: Why is 'the top predator is the most important species' an oversimplification?
options: Importance depends on which species is largest
Producers and decomposers are essential for energy entering and nutrients recycling
Top predators supply energy to the levels below them
Only herbivores matter to a food web
questions.explanation: Top predators can have outsized effects, but nothing works without producers capturing energy and decomposers returning nutrients.

questions.stem: Two ecosystems receive the same sunlight, but one supports far more animal life. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: Its food chains transfer nearly all energy between levels
Its producers grow faster because water and nutrients are more available
Its animals need less energy than usual
It has fewer decomposers, so more energy remains
questions.explanation: Productivity is limited by whatever is scarcest — often water or nutrients rather than light. Energy transfer efficiency does not vary enough to explain a large difference.

questions.stem: Why does eating plants directly feed more people than eating animals fed on those plants?
options: Meat cannot be digested by humans
Each transfer between levels loses most of the available energy
Plants contain more energy per kilogram than meat
Animals do not need to eat plants
questions.explanation: Adding a trophic level costs roughly 90% of the energy. This is an energy-flow argument, not a claim about the nutritional value of either food.

questions.stem: A lake is enriched by fertiliser runoff, algae bloom, and fish die. What is the best explanation?
options: Algae eat the fish
The extra algae block fish from swimming
Decomposing algae use up the oxygen dissolved in the water
The fertiliser is directly poisonous to fish
questions.explanation: The damage is indirect: the bloom eventually dies, decomposers multiply, and their respiration strips oxygen from the water. This is eutrophication.

questions.stem: Which action would most effectively protect a threatened species that needs a large territory?
options: Removing all other species from its range
Feeding the species in the wild
Protecting and reconnecting large areas of its habitat
Breeding more individuals in captivity alone
questions.explanation: Habitat area and connectivity are the binding constraint for wide-ranging species. Captive breeding has nowhere to release into if the habitat is gone.

questions.stem: What is a biotic factor?
options: A measure of how polluted a habitat is
A living part of an ecosystem, such as predators or plants
A non-living part of an ecosystem, such as temperature
The total energy entering an ecosystem
questions.explanation: Bio- means life. Biotic factors are the living components; abiotic factors are the physical ones.

questions.stem: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
options: The number of predators
The amount of grass
Competition between animals
Soil pH
questions.explanation: Soil pH is physical and non-living. Everything else listed involves organisms.
questions.teaching:
Ecosystems are described using two categories of factor, and sorting an unfamiliar factor into the right one is a standard skill.

One category covers the living components and their effects — predation, competition, disease, food availability. The other covers the non-living physical and chemical conditions: temperature, rainfall, light, wind, soil chemistry, salinity, water flow. Note that something produced by living things can still be non-living: a fallen log or the oxygen in water sits in the second category. Ask whether the factor is itself alive, not whether life was involved in producing it.

questions.stem: What does a pyramid of numbers show?
options: How many individual organisms are at each level of a food chain
How much energy is stored at each level
The total mass of organisms at each level
How fast energy moves between levels
questions.explanation: A pyramid of numbers counts individuals. Mass is a pyramid of biomass, and energy is a pyramid of energy.

questions.stem: What does a pyramid of biomass measure at each level?
options: The total mass of living material
The number of organisms
The number of species
The amount of sunlight absorbed
questions.explanation: Biomass is total mass of living material, so a huge tree and a single leaf are no longer counted the same way.

questions.stem: What is a trophic level?
options: The number of species in a habitat
The temperature range an organism tolerates
A feeding position in a food chain
The height an organism lives at
questions.explanation: Producers are the first trophic level, primary consumers the second, and so on.

questions.stem: What is migration?
options: The introduction of a species to a new country
The daily movement of an animal within its territory
A regular seasonal movement of animals between areas
The permanent extinction of a species
questions.explanation: Migration is regular and seasonal, usually following food or breeding conditions.

questions.stem: Which abiotic factor most directly limits plant growth in a desert?
options: Soil bacteria
Predator numbers
Water availability
The number of herbivores
questions.explanation: Deserts have ample light and warmth; water is the scarce factor.

questions.stem: What is a population?
options: The non-living parts of a habitat
All the individuals of one species in an area
All the living things in an area
All the species in a country
questions.explanation: A population is one species. All populations together make a community.

questions.stem: What is a community in ecological terms?
options: The soil, water and climate of an area
A group of animals that migrate together
All the populations of different species living in an area
One species living in an area
questions.explanation: Community covers all the living things. Add the abiotic surroundings and you have an ecosystem.

questions.stem: Which gas do producers take in for photosynthesis?
options: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Methane
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is taken in and oxygen released. Respiration runs the other way.
questions.teaching:
Photosynthesis takes in two raw materials and produces two products, and questions usually test which is which.

The raw materials are water, drawn up from the roots, and a gas taken in through the leaves. Light energy is used to combine them into glucose, and oxygen is released as a by-product. Respiration is the reverse: it consumes oxygen and glucose and releases the same gas back. That symmetry is the point — the gas taken in during photosynthesis is exactly the one that living things breathe out, which is what makes the carbon cycle work.

questions.stem: What is bioaccumulation?
options: The increase in species in a habitat
The spread of a species to new areas
The build-up of a substance in an organism's body over time
The growth of a population over time
questions.explanation: Substances that are not broken down or excreted accumulate — and concentrate further up the chain.

questions.stem: What is an apex predator?
options: The largest animal in a habitat
The fastest predator in a habitat
A predator that eats only plants
A predator with no natural predators of its own
questions.explanation: Apex predators sit at the top of the chain. Size and speed do not define the position.

questions.stem: Which process returns carbon from dead organisms to the atmosphere?
options: Migration
Predation
Decomposition
Photosynthesis
questions.explanation: Decomposers respire as they break material down, releasing carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: What does 'extinct' mean?
options: No individuals of the species remain anywhere
The species is rare
The species no longer lives in one country
The species has stopped migrating
questions.explanation: Extinction is total. Disappearing from one region while surviving elsewhere is local extinction.

questions.stem: Why is a pyramid of biomass usually a true pyramid shape even when a pyramid of numbers is not?
options: Numbers always increase up a chain
Biomass ignores producers
Total mass falls at each level even when one large producer supports many small consumers
Biomass counts only animals
questions.explanation: One oak tree makes a pyramid of numbers top-heavy, but the tree's mass still far exceeds that of the caterpillars it feeds.

questions.stem: Rising average temperatures cause a bird species to migrate two weeks earlier. Why might this be a problem?
options: Migration always harms a species
Warmer weather stops birds breeding
Its arrival may no longer match the peak of the food it depends on
Birds cannot fly in warm weather
questions.explanation: Species respond to warming at different rates, so timings that once matched can drift apart. This mismatch is one of the clearest documented effects of climate change on ecosystems.

questions.stem: Which change is an abiotic factor affecting a population?
options: A new predator arriving
A disease spreading through a herd
Competition for nesting sites
A drought reducing water in a river
questions.explanation: Water availability is physical. Predators, disease and competition all involve other organisms.

questions.stem: A lake warms by two degrees. Why might fish populations fall even with no change in food?
options: Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen
Warm water contains no nutrients
Fish stop reproducing above any temperature rise
Warm water is denser, so fish sink
questions.explanation: Oxygen solubility drops as temperature rises, so warming squeezes the oxygen available regardless of food supply.

questions.stem: Which is the best evidence that energy, not matter, is what runs out along a food chain?
options: Decomposers create new energy
Nutrients are recycled by decomposers, but energy is lost as heat at each transfer
Matter disappears at each level
Energy is recycled by producers
questions.explanation: Matter cycles; energy flows one way and leaves as heat. That asymmetry is why ecosystems need a continuous energy input from the Sun.

questions.stem: Habitat loss splits a forest into isolated patches. Which effect is most likely on a large predator?
options: Its population grows because prey is concentrated
It becomes a producer
It is unaffected, since it can fly between patches
Its population declines because each patch is too small to support it
questions.explanation: Wide-ranging species need large continuous territories. Fragmentation hits them hardest.

questions.stem: Why does removing a decomposer population eventually harm producers?
options: Nutrients stay locked in dead material instead of returning to the soil
Decomposers provide light to plants
Decomposers eat the herbivores
Producers eat decomposers directly
questions.explanation: Decomposition is the recycling step. Without it the nutrient supply to plants dries up.

questions.stem: A pest species is removed from an ecosystem entirely. Why might this backfire?
options: Predators that fed on it may decline, and species it competed with may increase unchecked
Removing a species never has side effects
The ecosystem will always recover exactly as before
Producers will die immediately
questions.explanation: Every species has connections in both directions. Removing one propagates through the web in ways that are hard to predict.

questions.stem: Which measurement would best show that an ecosystem is recovering after a fire?
options: The number of visitors to the area
Increasing species diversity and vegetation cover over successive surveys
A single count of one species
The temperature on one day
questions.explanation: Recovery is a trend across multiple measures and repeated surveys, not a snapshot of one variable.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes the effect of an introduced herbivore with no local predators?
options: It will become a producer
It competes with native herbivores while leaving plants untouched
Its population can grow rapidly and overgraze native plants
It will be eaten quickly and die out
questions.explanation: Without predation, population growth is limited only by food — which is why rabbits spread so destructively in Australia.

questions.stem: A food web shows an owl eating both mice and small birds. What does this indicate about its resilience?
options: It is a producer as well as a consumer
It occupies only one trophic level
A decline in one prey species need not be fatal, since it has an alternative
It will starve if either prey declines
questions.explanation: Multiple feeding options are what makes a web more robust than a single chain.

questions.stem: Why is a pyramid of energy always a true pyramid, unlike numbers or biomass?
options: Energy transfer is always less than 100 per cent, so every level holds less than the one below
Producers are always the most numerous organisms present, so the base is the widest by count
Energy is measured per unit area rather than per organism, which removes the effect of body size
Consumers are always physically larger, so fewer of them can be supported at each higher level
questions.explanation: The second law of thermodynamics guarantees loss at every transfer. Numbers and biomass can be inverted by size or timing; energy cannot.

questions.stem: A pyramid of biomass in the open ocean appears inverted, with less producer mass than consumer mass. Why?
options: Ocean consumers are producers
Energy flows upwards in the ocean only
The measurement must be wrong
Phytoplankton reproduce and are eaten so fast that their mass at any instant is small
questions.explanation: Biomass is a snapshot; productivity is a rate. Fast turnover means a small standing crop can support a much larger consumer mass.

questions.stem: Which explanation best links climate change to a decline in a mountain-top species?
options: The species migrates downhill and thrives
Warming increases rainfall, flooding mountain habitats
As warming pushes its suitable temperature range upslope, the habitat available shrinks to nothing
Mountains get colder as the climate warms
questions.explanation: Species can track a shifting climate horizontally, but on a mountain the escape route ends at the summit.

questions.stem: Which observation would most strongly support the claim that a predator controls a prey population?
options: The predator is found in the same habitat as the prey all year round and is seen feeding on it regularly
Prey numbers fall in every season the predator is present, whatever the weather has been in that season
Prey numbers rise sharply in areas where the predator has been removed, but not in comparable areas where it remains
Both populations rise and fall together over several years, with the predator's peak following the prey's
questions.explanation: A controlled comparison isolates the predator's effect. Coexistence and natural variation prove nothing on their own.

questions.stem: Why can a small change in an abiotic factor cause a large change in a food web?
options: Abiotic changes always reverse themselves
Food webs are unaffected by non-living factors
It can affect producers, and everything above them depends on producer output
Abiotic factors act only on top predators
questions.explanation: Effects at the base propagate upwards through every level that depends on it — a bottom-up cascade.

questions.stem: Why is the ten per cent rule described as an approximation rather than a law?
options: Actual transfer efficiency varies widely between ecosystems and between species
Energy transfer is always exactly ten per cent
It applies only to producers
It was never based on measurement
questions.explanation: Measured efficiencies range from around 1% to over 20% depending on the organisms and conditions. Ten per cent is a useful rough figure, not a constant.

questions.stem: Seasonal migration means some birds occupy two ecosystems a year. Why does this complicate conservation?
options: Migration means the birds belong to no ecosystem
Only the breeding ground matters
Protecting one end of the route is not enough if the other end or the stopovers are lost
Migratory birds do not need protection
questions.explanation: A migratory species depends on a chain of sites, so protection has to be international and cover the whole route.

questions.stem: What is a scavenger?
options: An animal that feeds on dead animals it did not kill
An animal that makes its own food
An animal that only eats plants
An organism that breaks down material chemically in the soil
questions.explanation: Scavengers such as crows and Tasmanian devils eat carrion. Decomposers work chemically at a much smaller scale.

questions.stem: What is a parasite?
options: An organism that lives on or in a host and harms it
An organism that hunts and kills prey
An organism that makes its own food
An organism that helps its host
questions.explanation: Parasites take resources from a living host. A relationship that helps both is mutualism.

questions.stem: What does 'carnivore' mean?
options: An organism that decomposes waste
An animal that eats other animals
An animal that eats plants
An animal that eats both
questions.explanation: Carnivores eat meat. Plant eaters are herbivores and mixed feeders are omnivores.

questions.stem: In a food chain, what always comes first?
options: A producer
A herbivore
A predator
A decomposer
questions.explanation: Chains begin with a producer, because that is where energy enters the system.
questions.teaching:
Food chains are drawn as arrows, and the arrows show the direction energy travels — from the eaten to the eater, which catches many people out.

Every chain has to start with something that brings energy into the living world in the first place, since consumers can only pass along energy that is already there. That role belongs to organisms capturing light energy and converting it into chemical energy. Without them there is nothing for anything else to eat. This is why the base of almost every ecosystem on Earth traces back to photosynthesis.

questions.stem: What is a food chain?
options: All the feeding links in an ecosystem
A list of species in a habitat
A count of animals over time
A single pathway showing what eats what
questions.explanation: A chain is one pathway; all the pathways together make a web.

questions.stem: Which organism would you expect in the largest numbers in a grassland?
options: Eagles
Foxes
Grass plants
Kangaroos
questions.explanation: Producers are most numerous because every level above depends on them and loses energy at each step.
questions.teaching:
Energy transfers between levels of a food web are very inefficient — only around 10% passes from one level to the next, with the rest lost as heat and in undigested material.

That inefficiency shapes the whole structure. Each level up can support far less living matter than the one below, which is why pyramids of numbers and biomass taper so sharply and why top predators are always rare. So when a question asks which organisms you would expect in the largest numbers, look for the level that captures energy directly rather than receiving it second or third hand.

questions.stem: What is meant by 'prey'?
options: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another
An animal that hunts others
A plant eaten by insects
An organism that decomposes waste
questions.explanation: Prey are hunted. An animal can be predator and prey at once.

questions.stem: What happens to most of the energy at each level of a food chain?
options: It is lost as heat, in movement and in waste
It is passed on completely to the next level
It is stored permanently in bones
It returns to the Sun
questions.explanation: Only a small fraction is stored as new body tissue. The rest is spent staying alive.

questions.stem: What is an invasive species?
options: A species that is close to extinction
An introduced species that spreads and damages the ecosystem
Any species that migrates seasonally
A species that is native to an area
questions.explanation: Not every introduced species becomes invasive — the label applies to those that spread and cause harm.

questions.stem: Which Australian animal is a well-known apex predator on land?
options: The wombat
The emu
The dingo
The kangaroo
questions.explanation: Dingoes sit at the top of many mainland food chains. The others are herbivores.
questions.teaching:
An apex predator sits at the top of its food web, with no natural predator of its own as an adult.

They tend to be large, long-lived and few in number, because the energy losses at every step of a food chain leave very little to support the top level. Their influence is disproportionate: removing one can let herbivore or mid-level predator numbers rise sharply and change the vegetation, an effect called a trophic cascade. In Australian ecosystems the debate about the top land predator and its effect on foxes and feral cats is exactly this argument.

questions.stem: In the chain phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → penguin, what is the penguin?
options: A primary consumer
A secondary consumer
A producer
A tertiary consumer
questions.explanation: Counting up from the producer: zooplankton primary, small fish secondary, penguin tertiary.

questions.stem: Why do decomposers appear in every food web, whatever the habitat?
options: Every organism eventually dies and must be broken down
Decomposers are eaten by all consumers
Decomposers produce energy for producers
Decomposers control predator numbers
questions.explanation: Death happens at every trophic level, so decomposition connects to all of them.

questions.stem: A drought reduces grass in a paddock. Predict the sequence of effects.
options: Herbivore numbers fall first, then predator numbers fall
Predator numbers fall first, then herbivores
Both rise together
Only decomposers are affected
questions.explanation: Effects travel up from the base with a lag. Predators feel it once their prey has declined.

questions.stem: Which is the better explanation for why top predators are usually rare?
options: They reproduce only once in a lifetime
They need less food than herbivores
They are hunted by other predators
Very little of the ecosystem's energy reaches their level
questions.explanation: Energy availability sets the ceiling on how many can be supported. Their rarity is a consequence of the pyramid, not of their biology alone.

questions.stem: Bees pollinate flowers while collecting nectar. What is this relationship called?
options: Parasitism
Predation
Competition
Mutualism, because both benefit
questions.explanation: The bee gets food; the plant gets pollinated. Both benefit, so it is mutualism.

questions.stem: Why can two similar species not usually occupy exactly the same niche in one place?
options: The two species would interbreed
One will out-compete the other for the shared resources
Two species can never live in the same habitat
Niches are assigned by classification
questions.explanation: Complete overlap means direct competition, and one typically prevails or the species diverge in how they use the resource.

questions.stem: A river is dammed and its seasonal flooding stops. Which effect on the food web is most likely?
options: Food chains become longer
Species that depend on floods to breed decline
All species increase because water is more reliable
Producers disappear entirely
questions.explanation: Many floodplain species time breeding to flooding. Removing the trigger removes the cue and the nursery habitat.

questions.stem: Which of these would increase the total energy available in an ecosystem?
options: More predators
Fewer decomposers
More trophic levels
More light and water, so producers grow faster
questions.explanation: Energy enters through producers, so the way to increase it is to increase primary production. Adding levels loses energy rather than adding it.

questions.stem: Why is it misleading to say a food web shows 'who is strongest'?
options: A web shows energy flow through feeding, not competition or strength
Food webs do show which animal is strongest
Strength determines trophic level
The largest animal is always at the top
questions.explanation: Arrows track energy. Some apex predators are small, and plenty of large animals are herbivores.

questions.stem: Rabbits are removed from an area where they had overgrazed. What is the likeliest outcome?
options: All native species immediately increase
The area becomes a desert
Native vegetation recovers, but predators that had switched to rabbits may decline
Native vegetation recovers and every predator population rises
questions.explanation: Removing an invasive species helps the plants it was eating but can leave predators that came to rely on it without food — one reason control programs are staged.

questions.stem: Why do ecologists sometimes measure productivity rather than biomass?
options: Productivity is easier to measure
Biomass counts only the largest organisms present
Productivity counts individuals
Productivity measures the rate energy is captured, which biomass at one moment can hide
questions.explanation: A fast-turnover community can have low standing biomass and very high productivity. The rate is what supports the levels above.

questions.stem: Why does a pesticide that is not broken down pose a greater risk than one that degrades quickly?
options: It persists and concentrates at each trophic level
It is more toxic to plants
It evaporates faster
It only affects decomposers
questions.explanation: Persistence is what allows bioaccumulation and biomagnification. DDT thinning raptor eggshells is the classic case.

questions.stem: Prey numbers in a valley fell sharply during a two-year drought, and the predator population fell the following year. What is the best explanation?
options: The predator caused the prey decline
The predator's decline caused the prey to decline afterwards
The prey ate the predator
The drought reduced the prey, and the predators then declined through loss of food
questions.explanation: The drought is an independent cause acting on the prey first, and the predators followed. Without that detail the order alone would not settle it, since over-hunting also leaves predators declining after their prey.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to protect a keystone species specifically?
options: It is always the rarest species
It has no predators
Its effect on the ecosystem is far larger than its abundance would suggest
It is always the largest species
questions.explanation: Keystone species hold structures together disproportionately — sea otters and kelp forests being the standard example.

questions.stem: An ecosystem model predicts that removing one species will have little effect. What would most improve confidence in that prediction?
options: Assuming the model is correct
Testing it against a real case where that species was lost and comparing outcomes
Running the same model again
Simplifying the model further
questions.explanation: A model gains credibility from being checked against observation. Repeating it changes nothing.
